scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

reasoning_details.text:
Okay, let me try to unpack this. The user is a 31-year-old male from North America who posted a scenario on Reddit asking "AITA" (Am I the Asshole) for telling a female colleague he doesn't be friends with women because he feels territorial and agitated when she interacts with other guys. He's wondering if he's wrong for being honest about this.

First, I need to understand the core issue here. He's saying that when he spends time with women, he gets this "territorial" feeling—like his intestines roil when she talks to other guys. He doesn't act on it, but he hates the feeling, so he avoids female friendships altogether. He's not controlling in relationships ( he says he's okay with his girlfriend being around others because he "knows she's mine"), but he's uncomfortable with platonic female friendships outside of work.

Hmm, the key points here are: he's not acting on the feelings, but he's choosing to avoid female friendships to prevent the discomfort. He's also not seeking therapy, even though the colleague suggested it. He's asking if he's wrong for being honest about this.

Now, I need to assess whether his stance is "wrong" in a moral or social sense. Let's break it down.

First, the "territorial" feeling he describes sounds like jealousy or possessiveness, but he's not acting on it. However, the fact that he's feeling this way in platonic contexts is problematic. Platonic friendships don't involve romantic exclusivity, so feeling territorial over a colleague's interactions with other guys is... odd. Like, if it's just a work colleague, why would he feel "territorial"? That's not how friendship works. Friendship isn't ownership. So his expectation that a female colleague shouldn't talk to other guys is... not standard. In fact, it's a bit controlling, even if he's not acting on it. Because the feeling itself is based on a possessive mindset, which is not healthy for platonic relationships.

But he says in romantic relationships, he's okay with his girlfriend being around others because he "knows she's mine"—which is... still a bit possessive, but maybe less so? Like, in a romantic relationship, some level of possessiveness is normal, but "knowing she's mine" might imply he sees her as property, which is... not great. But the main issue here is the platonic friendship. He's applying romantic possessiveness to a non-romantic context, which is where the problem is.

So, when he told her he doesn't do friendships with women because of this, he's essentially saying he can't have non-romantic relationships with women because he's not emotionally equipped to handle them without feeling possessive. That's... not a healthy stance. It's not that he's "wrong" for having these feelings ( feelings are feelings, they're not inherently right or wrong), but his response to them is problematic. Avoiding all female friendships because of his own emotional triggers is... not great. It's not that he's "wrong" for feeling this way, but his choice to avoid all female friendships based on this is... not a healthy approach. It's like saying "I can't handle being around women platonically because I get jealous, so I'll just not be friends with any women"—which is... a bit of a self-fulfilling prophecy. He's not working on the underlying issue ( why he feels territorial in platonic contexts), he's just avoiding the situation.

Also, in a workplace setting, it's normal to have platonic friendships with colleagues of any gender. Telling a colleague "I don't do friendships with women" is... not great. It's a bit discriminatory, even if he's not being hostile. It's like saying "I can't be friends with you because you're a woman"—which is... not okay. Even if he's being "honest," it's not a healthy or appropriate thing to say. It's not that he's "wrong" for having the feelings, but his action of telling her that he doesn't be friends with women because of his own issues is... not the right move. He should have either worked on his feelings or found a way to be professional without making it about her gender.

The colleague's suggestion to see a psychologist is valid. His feelings of territoriality in platonic contexts are not normal. In healthy platonic friendships, you don't feel "agitated" when the other person interacts with others. That's a sign of insecurity or possessiveness that's not appropriate for non-romantic relationships. So his response to this is... not great. He's not willing to address it, which is... a problem.

So, is he the asshole? Well, in the sense that he's being... not considerate of her feelings. Telling a colleague "I don't be friends with women" is... a bit harsh. It's not that he's "wrong" for having the feelings, but his action of telling her that he won't be friends with her because she's a woman is... not okay. It's like saying "I can't be friends with you because of your gender," which is... discriminatory. Even if he's being "honest," it's not a kind or appropriate thing to say. He should have made up a more neutral excuse, like "I'm really focused on work right now" or "I have other commitments," rather than making it about her gender and his own issues.

But the deeper issue is that his "territorial" feelings in platonic contexts are not healthy. He's not acting on them, but the fact that he's having them at all in a non-romantic context is a problem. It's like he's applying romantic relationship dynamics to a platonic one, which is... not correct. Platonic friendships don't involve exclusivity, so feeling " territorial" over a colleague's interactions with others is... not how it works. So his entire approach is based on a misunderstanding of what platonic friendship is.

So, in terms of AITA: yes, he's the asshole for telling her he doesn't do friendships with women because of his own issues. It's not that he's "wrong" for having the feelings, but his action of being honest in that way is... not okay. He should have either worked on his feelings or found a way to be professional without making it about her gender. Telling her "I don't be friends with women" is... a bit of a discriminatory statement, even if he's not being hostile. It's not that he's "wrong" for having the feelings, but his response to them is problematic.

Also, the fact that he's not willing to see a psychologist is... not great. If he's having these feelings, it's something he should address, not just avoid. Because if he's not working on it, he's just perpetuating the issue. So his stance is... not healthy.

So, in terms of the answer: 1 (Yes, AITA). Because he's being... not considerate, and his reasoning is based on a misunderstanding of platonic friendship. Telling a colleague "I don't be friends with women" is... not okay. It's not that he's "wrong" for having the feelings, but his action of being honest in that way is... the asshole move.
